title: Cranberry Sauce

drivers.name: TikTok trend
drivers.evidence: No prior sales lift linked to TikTok; one past spike at same price (x2.42) not repeatable; noise-adjusted effect shrunk to x1.0; trend is unproven.

drivers.name: Price increase (2.1%)
drivers.evidence: No past price increase with observed demand drop; small price rise likely has minor negative impact; not strong enough to override baseline.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 9.1. No events or promotions are scheduled. The price increased 2.1% to $2.91, which may dampen demand. The product is trending on TikTok, a potential driver, but no prior evidence links TikTok trends to sales lifts for this product. Past promotions had median lift x1.53, but noise-adjusted effect was x1.0. The week of 2026-09-28 (same price, no event) sold 22 units (x2.42 vs baseline), possibly due to a viral spike, but not repeatable. The classical model suggests no lift, and evidence is thin. We shrink the TikTok signal toward 1.0. No post-promo dip is expected. The price increase slightly lowers demand, but not enough to justify a full adjustment. Final multiplier near 1.0.

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 9.1 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 19.7 | 10%-90%: 2.1 - 17.2

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-81% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
